newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Germany not seeking hegemony in EU.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germany not seeking hegemony in EU.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, outlining his policies before the EU's Dublin summit, on Thursday said Germany did not seek hegemony in Europe but wanted a flexible approach to allow more integration wherever possible.

Addressing parliament a day before the summit, Kohl said he was confident the European Union would agree on a stability pact which Bonn wants to ensure the future single European currency -- the euro -- enjoys long-term stability.
He underlined Germany's interest in tightening cooperation in fighting organised crime, having more majority voting in the EU and improving the bloc's performance in foreign affairs.

In an aside to critics abroad, the chancellor said Germany, as the biggest member in the EU, was often suspected of wanting a dominant position, especially when it called for structural reforms like changing the weighting of votes in the council.
"We do not seek to exercise hegemonic influence, as some charge," he said. "We don't want to see a Europe where the big countries have the say and the smaller ones are appendages.
"This is not our idea of federalism in Germany and it is not our idea of federalism in Europe."

Germany has run into criticism from its EU partners for insisting on a stability pact with automatic penalties for countries participating in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) which overstep strict budget constraints after monetary union starts in 1999.

Calling Europe a "whole bouquet with all its bright colours", Kohl called for more subsidiarity in the EU -- deciding some matters at local level rather than in Brussels -- but added that Germans must understand this was difficult for others.
"Our partners will not automatically accept our ideas because they have completely different traditions," he said.
Kohl said Germany was still interested in a so-called "flexibility clause" it proposed with France that would allow some EU members to integrate faster than others.
If this was not possible in important areas like fighting crime, he said, willing member states should agree to push ahead by themselves and try to make this EU policy later on.
As for the EU's planned Economic and Monetary Union, Kohl stressed he wanted it to start on time in 1999 and to adhere to the Maastricht Treaty's strict economic convergence criteria.
"I am confident that we will find a solution that will show all citizens the determination of the European Union to create a euro with long-term stability," he said.
He also expected EU members to agree on the powers of the new European Central Bank but gave no details.

Seeking common ground with British critics of plans to replace consensus voting at EU summits, Kohl suggested member states could decide issues by majority voting except for specific issues that they agree to exempt from the rule.

He reiterated his call for the EU to expand eastwards as it deepens integration among its current 15 members, adding: "It is completely inconceivable that Poland should not become a member of the European Union."
Speakers from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens supported the single currency and underlined widespread concerns about its stability.
Greens leader Joschka Fischer criticised Bonn's position as "ritualised stability fetishism" that had more to do with domestic politics than with economic realities in Europe.

He said Bonn's insistence on the tightest possible stability pact was creating more unemployment in France and putting President Jacques Chirac under such pressure that he could lose his pro-EU majority.
"That is the real message of Nuremberg," he said, referring to a France-German summit held in the German city on Monday.
